answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator found “no substantive support” for Margaret Mead. The exact wording first appears in print in 1979 — the year after Mead died — in a Doubleday compilation of comic maxims, filed under the label “Meade’s Maxim,” spelled with an e and tied to no identified person. QI tentatively ascribes the earlier, rougher 1971 version of the joke to Dallas newspaperman Jim Wright.

source.trailTitle: How a maxim became a Mead quote
trail: 13 March 1971 — the earliest evidence located by researchers is a rougher form of the joke. Writing in The Dallas Morning News column “On Second Thought,” assistant editorial director Jim Wright mocks the bestseller The Greening of America and its young revolutionaries with the question “How can I be unique just like everybody else?” Quote Investigator ↗

1979 — the exact modern wording reaches print for the first time, in John Peers’s compilation 1,001 Logical Laws from Doubleday, where it is filed not under “Mead” but as “Meade’s Maxim” and credited to nobody in particular. Open Library record ↗ Margaret Mead had died in November 1978. Wikipedia ↗

1989 — the anthropologist’s name attaches. Paul Dickson’s The New Official Rules prints “Mead’s Distinction. You are totally unique, just like everyone else” and credits Margaret Mead; a St. Petersburg Times panel by Don Addis that December runs the same wording under “Margaret Meade.” Quote Investigator ↗

Today — Wikiquote lists the line among Mead’s Disputed quotations, noting the 1979 “Meade’s Maxim” designation was “not linked directly to Margaret Mead” and that there is “no definitely documented evidence” she said it. Wikiquote ↗

source.rightsNote: No rights status can honestly be asserted for this sentence, because it has no identified author. Its earliest located printing is quote page 155 of John Peers’s 1,001 Logical Laws (Doubleday, 1979) — a post-1930 book still in copyright as a compilation — but there the line is filed under a jokey label rather than credited to anyone, and it may well have circulated in speech before that. It is certainly not Margaret Mead’s, and it is not demonstrably public domain.

author.heading: Who the joke actually belongs to
author.metaLine: Assistant editorial director, The Dallas Morning News · wrote the 1971 version of the quip
author.bio: Quote Investigator identifies Jim Wright as an assistant editorial director for The Dallas Morning News, and “tentatively” credits him with the earliest located version of the joke — a March 1971 column taking aim at the counterculture bestseller The Greening of America. He is a newspaperman, not the Texas congressman of the same name. Even so, Wright owns the idea rather than the sentence: the polished wording that circulates today first shows up eight years later, in a joke compilation, with no author attached to it.

misattribution.heading: How Mead’s name got welded to it
misattribution.intro: Margaret Mead is one of the internet’s most dependable magnets for warm, tidy sayings she never published. This one seems to have arrived by a clerical accident — a single stray letter.

items.why: Wikiquote files the line under Disputed, recording that it “was designated ‘Meade’s Maxim’ in a 1979 book… and not linked directly to Margaret Mead,” and that there is “no definitely documented evidence of this.” Wikiquote ↗

Quote Investigator’s conjecture is that the Mead ascription grew out of a misreading of the 1979 label, which is spelled Meade. QI adds that Peers sometimes chose such labels for comic effect, so “the saying may not even be solidly linked to someone named Meade.” Quote Investigator ↗

The two 1989 sightings that first put Mead’s name on the joke both read “You are totally unique, just like everyone else” — Paul Dickson’s The New Official Rules as “Mead’s Distinction,” and a St. Petersburg Times panel by Don Addis that spells her “Margaret Meade.” The “absolutely” wording on today’s posters comes from the 1979 book, not from them. Quote Investigator ↗

A March 2001 newspaper column written in the voice of the Red Green television character ran “Always remember you’re unique, just like everyone else” under his name; QI notes the comedy team behind the show employed the quip when it was already in circulation. Quote Investigator ↗

misattribution.truthLine: The closest thing to an author is a Dallas newspaperman. Quote Investigator finds “no substantive support” for Margaret Mead and says the 1971 version of the joke — “How can I be unique just like everybody else?” — “can tentatively be ascribed to Jim Wright.” Quote Investigator ↗

context.heading: An insult that became a compliment
lead: The joke started life as a sneer. In a March 1971 Dallas Morning News column, assistant editorial director Jim Wright took aim at The Greening of America ↗, Charles A. Reich’s 1970 bestseller about a rising generation remaking the country, and asked the deflating question “How can I be unique just like everybody else?” ↗ The target was mass nonconformity — a whole cohort declaring its individuality in unison.

The version that sells posters and graduation cards points the other way. It is reassurance, not mockery, and it travels under the name of Margaret Mead ↗, the cultural anthropologist who died in November 1978. It fits her public voice well enough that it stuck. It is also, as far as anyone has documented, not hers: the sentence first surfaces in print the following year, in a book of comic maxims, credited to a “Meade” who may never have existed.
context.detailsSummary: But a student says he heard her say it
detailsBody: Wikiquote carries one piece of anecdotal testimony, flagged as needing a citation. Alex Randall, describing himself as a graduate student with Mead from 1974 to 1977, is quoted saying: “I heard her say these words in a class as a graduate student. I took them down as notes for the class. I can’t say they were unique to her, but she certainly said this.” Wikiquote, Disputed ↗

Take that at face value and it still does not make Mead the author. The quip was already in a Dallas newspaper in 1971, before those classes; and Randall himself allows that the words were not unique to her. Repeating a good line in a lecture is how sayings spread, not how they start — and it is exactly how a teacher’s name ends up welded to one.
context.pull: Written to mock the crowd. Sold to comfort the individual.
